How it works

The model guesses how text sounds, so it trips on numbers and names

Text“Six forty-two.”
→
Modelguesses chunks of sound
→
Sound chunksaudio tokens, 12–50 steps per second
→
Decoderrebuilds the waveform
→
Sound24,000–48,000 numbers per second
Line 1 of our script, real waveform · 3.9 s
Compression: a second of audio is tens of thousands of numbers. The model works with a short summary of a few dozen chunks; the decoder expands it back into a waveform.
What is not inside: a rulebook for reading. The model learned how text usually sounds, so it most often errs on numbers, names and abbreviations.

The L05 failure clipprompt has no dialogue either
▶ audio in the HTML version
Heard in Veo’s audio“Continue straight for 200 meters, then your destination is on the left.”
Provides: street noise, rain, footsteps, in sync with the picture. But you pay for it: Veo 3.1 on Vertex AI is $0.40/s with audio, $0.20/s without.

Voice-over script: text, timing and a word budget for each shot

ShotTimeVoice-overWords / lengthSound effects
0–8 s“6:42. Order 417 is picked up, still hot.”11 / 3.9 scafe: room noise, cups
7.5–15.5 s“Rain on the avenue. The route skips the bridge.”9 / 2.7 srain, tyres on puddles
15–23 s“12 minutes to the door. Anna is on her way.”10 / 2.7 ssoft UI sound
Music: one bed for all shots, lo-fi, no vocals
≈ 3.2 words/s
our voice: faster than plan; it fits only because the lines are short. Plan: 2–2.5 words/s
An 8 s shot ≈ 6 s of speech (about 1 s of silence at each cut) × 2–2.5 words/s = 12–15 words. If it does not fit, cut the text; do not speed up the voice.

Mixing: voice on top, background ducked, loudness normalised

Voicetext-to-speech
Veo audiovideo sound, ducked under the voice
MusicMusicGen
Mix−14.4 LUFS · −2.2 dBTP
  • Ducking: the background drops automatically while the voice speaks.
  • Loudness −14 LUFS (a loudness unit that follows the ear): the Spotify and YouTube norm; TV uses −23.
  • Peak in the final file no higher than −1 dBTP, otherwise encoding makes it crackle. Set the limiter to −2 for headroom, see right.
No code, Audacity (free): import the three tracks → background: Effect › Auto Duck → Loudness Normalization −14 LUFS → Limiter −2 dB (headroom: AAC in the video adds ~0.5 dB) → WAV into CapCut or Clipchamp.

  • “Here’s your order.”: the mix: Veo’s invented line leaks through
  • “642” instead of “6:42”: speech-to-text formatting; the voice said it correctly
18.5%
word error rate (WER) = (substitutions + deletions + insertions) / words in the script
3 / 4 automatically → 4 / 4 after listening
critical terms correct (time, order number, minutes, name)

Hands-on with an agent

A coding agent installs Qwen3-TTS locally and clones a voice

Prompt for a coding agent: Codex in ChatGPT or Antigravity (free, with limits), Claude Code (paid)
Install the open-weight text-to-speech model Qwen3-TTS (Qwen/Qwen3-TTS-12Hz-0.6B-Base, Apache-2.0) in C:\ai\qwen-tts-demo and clone MY voice.
0. My sample: my_voice.m4a from Windows Sound Recorder, 10 s, and my_voice.txt with its exact text. Convert the sample to 24 kHz mono WAV with ffmpeg.
1. Check the graphics card and its memory, system memory, free disk (~5 GB). Tell me what fits: 0.6B or 1.7B, graphics card or processor.
2. Create a separate Python environment there; install qwen-tts and soundfile.
3. Download the model from Hugging Face and show where the files are.
4. Write clone.py and say in my voice, in English: “Six forty-two. Order four one seven is picked up, still hot.” → line1.wav.
5. Run it, report the time, upload nothing to the internet.

Acceptance

Both our versions failed acceptance: here is the checklist

The same items are the homework rubric. On the right, the real result for our version.
  1. Words match the script: speech-to-text + critical terms list
  2. Pronunciation of names, numbers, terms: checked by ear
  3. Timing: each line fits its shot and is not cut by a transition
  4. Mix: voice is clear, background ducked, no stray speech
  5. Loudness −14 ± 1 LUFS; true peak ≤ −1 dB (dBTP)
  6. Rights: voice and music licence, consent, “AI-generated” label

Risks

Risks and voice consent: cloning, labelling, law

Library or designed voice
allowed under the service licence, with an “AI-generated” label
Your own voice, a colleague’s clone
written consent: purpose, where, how long, how to withdraw
A client’s, manager’s or public figure’s voice
not without written consent and legal review; voices are used for fraud
How services check consent for a clone
  • OpenAI, Google: the voice owner records a consent phrase. Azure: access on application.
  • ElevenLabs Professional: the owner reads a verification text aloud; Instant: a checkbox only.
  • Open-weight models (Qwen3-TTS, Chatterbox): clone from 3–10 s, no checks at all.
EU AI Act, Art. 50: from 2 August 2026, synthetic audio and deepfakes must be labelled; fines up to €15M or 3% of turnover. OpenAI requires telling listeners the voice is AI-generated. Google embeds an invisible SynthID watermark in audio from its own models.
